difficulty: Hard - '10x in 3 years' is mathematically impossible on revenue alone, so the candidate must spot this, reframe the goal, and build a credible bottom-up path against JioHotstar's scale and India's low willingness to pay

exact_prompt: "You are the Head of Netflix India. Leadership wants you to grow the business 10x in the next 3 years. What is your strategy?"
source_and_verification: Reported (Meesho PM interview, per the casebook outline). Close public matches: PracHub 'Netflix in India: Diagnose Slow Growth and Plan a Tenfold Expansion' (https://prachub.com/interview-questions/netflix-in-india-diagnose-slow-growth-and-plan-a-tenfold-expansion), which asks the candidate to clarify whether 10x means paid subscribers, viewers, revenue or viewing time; technomanagers101 'How would you increase the market penetration of Netflix in developing countries?' (2022, https://technomanagers101.blogspot.com/2022/10/How%20would%20you%20increase%20the%20market%20penetration%20of%20Netflix%20in%20developing%20countries.html); a related 'PM Wargame: 10X Netflix UK's revenue' (https://alexdebecker.substack.com/p/pm-wargame-10x-netflix-uks-revenue). No Meesho-specific public write-up was found on NextLeap, AmbitionBox or Glassdoor; the Meesho attribution is from the casebook source list. Year reported: [uncertain] 2024-2026.
context_as_of: As of Nov 2026: (1) Netflix Q3 2026 (reported 20 Oct 2026): global revenue $12.87 bn (+12% YoY), 2026 revenue guidance about $51.1 bn; Netflix called Q3 2026 its best-ever quarter for India paid net additions, with India revenue up about 18% YoY (FX-neutral) and viewing hours up about 24%, crediting the local slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart (Inc42, Oct 2026: https://inc42.com/buzz/netflix-credits-flipkart-bundle-indian-shows-for-record-q3-subscriber-additions/ ; MediaNews4U: https://www.medianews4u.com/netflix-india-posts-record-paid-net-additions-in-q3-2026-revenue-grows-18-on-strong-content-slate/). Netflix no longer reports subscriber counts (stopped from Q1 2025), so India subscriber numbers are third-party estimates. (2) Netflix Entertainment Services India LLP FY25: revenue from operations Rs 3,769 cr (+32%), net profit Rs 85 cr (+63%), per MCA filings (Inc42: https://inc42.com/features/netflix-flips-its-india-script/). A Jan 2026 Business Standard piece put Netflix India at 16 mn+ subscribers, about 50 mn viewers and close to Rs 4,000 cr revenue. (3) Competition: JioHotstar (Reliance-Disney JV, merged Feb 2025) is the scale leader with IPL and ICC cricket; HSBC estimates about 300 mn paying subscriptions in 2025 versus about 65 mn for Prime Video and about 20 mn for Netflix (cited via texxr.com and Ragalahari, Jan 2026); JioHotstar's 'Tadka' short-format service reportedly hit 100 mn users within two months of launch (RIL AGM 2026, Business Today: https://www.businesstoday.in/latest/corporate/story/ril-agm-2026-jiohotstars-tadka-hits-100-million-users-in-under-two-months-of-its-launch-538121-2026-06-19). Prime Video is bundled with Amazon Prime and ships ads by default. (4) Netflix India pricing: Mobile Rs 149, Basic Rs 199, Standard Rs 499, Premium Rs 649 per month (Netflix Help Center: https://help.netflix.com/en/node/24926/in); prices unchanged since the Dec 2021 cut. Netflix's ad-supported plan is not confirmed as launched in India; Netflix said it will bring its ad tier to 15 more countries in 2027 (Q3 2026 earnings coverage), and India is a natural candidate. Telco bundles exist with Jio and Airtel prepaid and postpaid plans. Stale-risk flags: JioHotstar subscriber counts vary hugely by definition (paid vs bundled vs users); the Flipkart bundle details and the India ad-tier status should be re-checked before use.
regulatory_context: (1) IT Rules 2021 (Digital Media Ethics Code): OTT platforms self-classify content by age (U, U/A 7+, 13+, 16+, A), need parental locks and a three-tier grievance mechanism; MIB has pressed platforms on obscenity and in 2025 banned several smaller adult-content apps - Netflix's bolder content strategy carries takedown and reputational risk. (2) Draft Broadcasting Services (Regulation) Bill (2023-24 drafts) could bring OTT under a content evaluation committee regime; status uncertain. (3) RBI e-mandate rules for recurring payments: card and UPI Autopay mandates need additional factor authentication above Rs 15,000 and pre-debit notifications - not a problem at Rs 149-649 but it shapes renewal UX, and UPI Autopay is the key mass payment rail. (4) DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules (notified Nov 2025, phased compliance) govern consent for using viewing and purchase data in bundles such as Flipkart or telco partnerships. (5) Sports rights: cricket media rights are auctioned by BCCI/ICC (JioStar holds IPL digital rights to 2027); the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act 2007 forces sharing of national-importance events with Doordarshan, which reduces exclusivity for any big live cricket bid. (6) FDI: 100% FDI allowed in OTT/digital content (non-news) under the automatic route. Mark: the Broadcasting Bill status is uncertain.

framework_applied: Product Strategy: Clarify, Context (4 pillars), Recommend (frameworks.md section 2); this is a strategic plan question ('what should we do'). Step 1 Clarify - pin down what '10x' means (revenue vs paid members vs reach), the baseline (about 20 mn paid accounts, about 50 mn viewers, about Rs 4,000 cr revenue), the 3-year horizon, and constraints (can we cut price, run ads, bid for cricket, accept lower ARPU and short-term losses). Step 2 Context - Company positioning: premium, global-plus-local storytelling brand with the highest ARPU in India but low reach; quick TAM check shows 10x revenue (about Rs 40,000 cr) would exceed India's entire video subscription pool, so revenue 10x is unrealistic and reach 10x is the only credible reading. Customers: urban premium households are saturated; the unserved are Tier 2/3, regional-language, mobile-first, price-sensitive families who get video free via YouTube or bundled via telcos. Competition: JioHotstar (cricket plus Rs 1-per-day pricing plus Jio distribution), Prime Video (bundled with shopping), YouTube (free, ad-supported), Zee5/SonyLIV/Aha/Sun NXT (regional), short-form and micro-drama apps. Market forces: content and talent costs rising (supplier power), very high buyer price sensitivity, low switching costs, distribution controlled by telcos and super-apps, cricket rights out of reach (JioStar to 2027). Step 3 Recommend - reframe the goal as 10x reach (20 mn to about 200 mn members) and about 3-4x revenue, delivered through four engines: an India ad tier, distribution bundles (telcos, Flipkart, others), a regional-first content machine, and mobile/short-format plus event programming; phased rollout with clear triggers and guardrails on premium ARPU and brand.
clarifying_questions: Q: What should grow 10x - revenue, paid subscriptions, or total viewers/reach? A: Leadership says 'the business'. You decide which metric is the right North Star, but justify it.
Q: What is the baseline I should use? A: Assume about 20 mn paid accounts, about 50 mn monthly viewers (people, not accounts), and about Rs 4,000 cr annual revenue.
Q: Is the 3-year horizon fixed, and is short-term profitability a constraint? A: Three years is fixed. India can run at a modest loss for two years if the path to profit is clear.
Q: Am I allowed to change pricing, including an ad-supported tier or lower prices? A: Yes. Global has an ad tech stack; India launch is your call. Avoid damaging the premium brand.
Q: Can I bid for live sports such as cricket? A: IPL and ICC digital rights are locked with JioStar until at least 2027. One-off events and non-cricket sports are open.
Q: What content budget do I have? A: Assume the India content budget can roughly double over three years, but every rupee must show viewing per rupee.
Q: Are partnerships (telcos, e-commerce, device makers) in scope? A: Yes. Netflix already has Jio and Airtel bundles and a new Flipkart loyalty bundle.
Q: Which user segment matters most to leadership? A: No preference; they want India to be a top-3 Netflix market by members.
interviewer_data_reveals: Exhibit 1 (illustrative, consistent with public estimates) - Netflix India member mix today: Mobile Rs 149: 35%; Basic Rs 199: 20%; Standard Rs 499: 25%; Premium Rs 649: 10%; telco-bundled: 10%. Blended ARPU about Rs 300-330 per month (approx Rs 3,900-4,000 cr annualised on about 10-11 mn effective paying accounts plus bundles; real reported FY25 revenue Rs 3,769 cr, MCA via Inc42).
Exhibit 2 (illustrative) - Geography of paid accounts: Top 8 metros 68%; Tier 2 cities 22%; Tier 3 and rural 10%. Population share of OTT users is roughly the inverse (metros about 30%).

Exhibit 3 (illustrative) - Viewing by language (share of hours): Hindi originals and licensed 38%; English/international 30%; Korean and Japanese 12%; South Indian languages (Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada) 15%; other Indian languages 5%. Note: South Indian films post-theatrical are the fastest-growing slice.

Exhibit 4 (illustrative) - Funnel for a non-member who opens the app via a trial or bundle offer: sign-up page reached 100; plan selection 55; payment started 35; payment success 28; still active after 3 months 16. Top exit reason at plan selection: 'too expensive versus JioHotstar/Prime'.

Exhibit 5 (real, third-party) - Market share of India paid subscriptions 2025 (HSBC): JioHotstar about 300 mn, Prime Video about 65 mn, Netflix about 20 mn; about 24% of OTT users pay for content. Ormax counts about 148 mn active paid subscriptions; FICCI-EY about 216 mn across about 143 mn households. Source definitions differ.

Exhibit 6 (illustrative) - Bundle pilots: Flipkart loyalty bundle members convert to direct paid after the bundle period at 22%; telco bundle (Jio postpaid) members watch 40% fewer hours than direct members but churn 50% less while bundled.

Exhibit 7 (illustrative) - Ad-tier test in a comparable emerging market: at a price about 40% below the cheapest ad-free plan, 55% of new sign-ups picked the ad tier, cannibalisation of existing ad-free members was under 5%, and ad ARPU added about 60% of the subscription fee within 12 months.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: You are the Head of Netflix India. Leadership wants 10x growth in 3 years. What's your strategy?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Big goal, so I want to be precise before I build anything. I'll clarify what '10x' means and the constraints, then look at Netflix's position, Indian customers, competition and market forces, and end with a recommendation and a phased plan. Okay?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Go ahead.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: First, 10x of what - revenue, paid accounts, or viewers? And what baseline should I assume?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Leadership said 'the business'. Assume about 20 million paid accounts, about 50 million viewers and about Rs 4,000 crore revenue. You choose the metric but justify it.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Then a quick sanity check. 10x revenue is Rs 40,000 crore. FICCI-EY puts India's whole digital video market - ads plus subscriptions - at roughly Rs 38,000 crore. So 10x revenue would mean Netflix alone being bigger than the entire market in three years. That's not a plan, that's a wish. 10x members, from 20 to about 200 million, is ambitious but has a precedent: JioHotstar reached a few hundred million subscriptions with cricket and Jio distribution. So I'll propose 10x reach as the North Star and about 3-4x revenue as the financial commitment. Can I check the constraints? Can I change pricing, add ads, and lose money short term?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Yes on pricing and ads, just don't damage the premium brand. India can run at a modest loss for two years. Cricket rights are locked with JioStar until 2027.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Got it. Now context, starting with Netflix itself. Netflix's model is subscription first, with ads as a newer second engine, about $2.7 billion globally in 2026. In India it's the premium brand: highest ARPU, strong urban reputation, global plus Indian originals, and a good product. The weakness is reach. At about 20 million accounts it's a fraction of JioHotstar, and the Rs 149 entry price is still 2-3x what mass India pays for video. Opportunity cost matters too: every rupee spent on India could earn a higher return in Korea or LatAm, so the plan must show improving unit economics.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Here's our member mix and geography.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 1: Mobile Rs 149 is 35% of members, Basic 20%, Standard 25%, Premium 10%, telco-bundled 10%. Exhibit 2: 68% of paid accounts are in the top 8 metros, 22% Tier 2, 10% Tier 3 and rural.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
That tells me the metro premium segment is largely captured, and 90% of the next 180 million members have to come from Tier 2/3 and from families who pay little or nothing today. Let me segment customers:
- Segment A: Metro premium households (about 20-25 mn). Pain: content fatigue, password-sharing limits. Already served.
- Segment B: Aspirational Tier 1-2 mobile-first young adults (about 60-80 mn). Pain: price, 480p on mobile, wants Hindi and South content plus K-drama.
- Segment C: Tier 2/3 family TV households with a new smart TV or Jio/Airtel fibre (about 40-50 mn and growing fast). Pain: needs regional-language films and family-safe shows; pays for one service, usually the cricket one.
- Segment D: Bharat free viewers on YouTube and short video (300 mn+). Pain: won't pay, data-conscious, vertical-video habit.
B and C are the swing segments for 10x; D is reachable only through ads and short formats.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What about content? Exhibit 3: Hindi is 38% of hours, English/international 30%, Korean and Japanese 12%, South Indian 15%, other Indian languages 5%. South is the fastest growing.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
That fits segment C. Telugu, Tamil and Malayalam audiences watch the most films per person, and post-theatrical film rights are the cheapest viewing per rupee. Our regional share is too low for a 200 million plan. Now the competitive landscape:
| Player | Why users pick it | Where it falls short |
| JioHotstar | Cricket, Disney and Star library, low price, Jio distribution | Weaker prestige originals, cluttered UX, ads heavy |
| Prime Video | Bundled with free delivery | Ads by default, thin originals cadence |
| YouTube | Free, everything, vertical | No premium long-form |
| Zee5 / SonyLIV / Aha / Sun NXT | Regional depth | Small budgets, weak tech |
| Micro-drama apps, JioHotstar Tadka | Cheap, snackable vertical drama | Low quality ceiling |
The trend I'd flag is short-form and micro-drama: Tadka reportedly hit 100 million users in two months. That's attention we compete with.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: And market forces?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Four quick ones. Supplier power is high: star fees and South film rights are bid up by JioHotstar and Prime. Buyer power is very high: price-sensitive customers who switch monthly, around IPL for example. Distribution is a chokepoint: Jio, Airtel and Flipkart control access to hundreds of millions of wallets, so partners have leverage over us. Cost to enter mass India is mostly content plus customer acquisition; the tech is already built. So the winning moves are distribution and price architecture, not just more shows.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Here's our sign-up funnel. Exhibit 4: 100 reach the sign-up page, 55 reach plan selection, 35 start payment, 28 succeed, and 16 are still active after three months. The top exit reason at plan selection is 'too expensive'.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: So price is the biggest leak, and payment success at 80% also has room - UPI Autopay mandate failures are a known issue. The 16% three-month survival tells me content fit for new segments matters too. Price, payments and regional content all show up in the data.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: We've also tested bundles. Exhibit 6: Flipkart loyalty bundle members convert to direct paid at 22% after the bundle ends. Telco bundle members watch 40% less but churn 50% less.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: That's useful. Bundles are cheap acquisition with decent conversion, but bundled members are lighter viewers, so ARPU per bundle seat has to be negotiated to cover that, and we need in-app hooks to deepen engagement. One more question: do you have any read on an ad tier?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 7, from a comparable emerging market: an ad tier priced about 40% below the cheapest ad-free plan got 55% of new sign-ups, under 5% cannibalisation, and ad revenue added about 60% of the subscription fee within a year.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
Then here's my recommendation. The reframe: Netflix India should go from 'the premium streamer for metro India' to 'the second screen in every Indian home' - 10x reach, 3-4x revenue, with premium kept intact at the top. Four engines:
1. Price ladder with ads: launch a Rs 79-99 mobile-with-ads plan and a Rs 149-199 TV-with-ads plan, keeping ad-free plans unchanged. Annual UPI Autopay plans, and a sachet option such as a weekend pass.
2. Distribution bundles: expand Jio/Airtel/Vi bundles to the prepaid mass tiers on an ad tier, scale the Flipkart loyalty bundle, and add device-maker (smart TV, Android OEM) and DTH/fibre bundles.
3. Regional-first content machine: shift content spend so South and other Indian languages reach about 35-40% of hours; more post-theatrical South films, dubbing and subtitles into 8+ languages, and family-safe shows for TV households.
4. Mobile and event layer: a vertical clips feed for discovery (not a micro-drama clone), plus live events that don't need cricket - comedy specials, music concerts, WWE, boxing, and Netflix's global live slate.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Show me how that adds up to 200 million.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
Bottom-up by Year 3 (illustrative):
| Source | Members | Monthly ARPU | Annual revenue |
| Direct ad-free | 25 mn | Rs 330 | about Rs 9,900 cr |
| Direct ad tier (mobile + TV) | 65 mn | Rs 90 sub + Rs 40 ads | about Rs 10,100 cr |
| Telco bundles (ad tier) | 70 mn | Rs 35 wholesale + Rs 20 ads | about Rs 4,600 cr |
| Commerce/OEM bundles | 40 mn | Rs 40 | about Rs 1,900 cr |
| Total | 200 mn | | about Rs 26,000 cr gross |
That gross figure is too optimistic, so I'd haircut it for churn, partial-year ramp and ad fill rates by about 50%, landing near Rs 12,000-15,000 crore - about 3-4x today. That's consistent with my framing: 10x reach, 3-4x revenue.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Why not just slash the price of the ad-free plans?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Because it reprices the whole base. If 20 million members drop from about Rs 330 to Rs 149, we lose more than half our revenue before winning anyone new. The ad tier price-discriminates: price-sensitive users trade attention for a lower price, and premium users keep paying for no ads. Exhibit 7 suggests cannibalisation is low.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What's the phasing?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Year 1, foundation: launch the India ad tier on mobile and TV, fix the payments funnel (UPI Autopay retries, annual plans), sign the mass telco prepaid bundle, and double down on the South film pipeline. Target about 45-50 million members. Year 2, distribution scale: OEM and fibre bundles, regional originals in 4 South languages, vertical discovery feed, first big India live events. Target about 100-120 million. Year 3, monetisation depth: ad products for Indian brands (D2C, FMCG, quick commerce), shoppable ads with partners, price increases on premium tiers. Target about 200 million. The trigger to push harder on ads is ad ARPU reaching about 40% of the subscription fee; the trigger to slow down is premium churn rising.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What risks are you accepting?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Three main ones. (1) Brand dilution: ads and cheap tiers could make Netflix feel like 'just another app'. Mitigation: low ad load (about 4 minutes per hour), no ads on the premium tier, and the flagship originals stay premium. (2) Bundled members who never watch: we'd be paying for vanity metrics. Mitigation: wholesale pricing tied to activation, and the North Star counts monthly active members, not just accounts. (3) Content cost inflation as JioHotstar and Prime bid up South films. Mitigation: multi-year output deals with regional producers and more in-house regional originals. Also a regulatory risk: content rules under the IT Rules mean bolder originals can face takedown demands, so standards and practices need to stay strong.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What if JioHotstar responds by bundling for free with every Jio plan?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Then we shouldn't fight on price. We'd lean on Airtel, Vi, Flipkart and OEMs, and differentiate on what JioHotstar is weakest at: prestige storytelling, global content and product quality. Many households will hold two services - one for cricket and one for stories. Our job is to be the second one.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: How would you measure success along the way?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: North Star: monthly active members (accounts with at least 2 hours of viewing a month). Supporting metrics: share of new members from Tier 2/3, regional share of hours, ad ARPU per member, bundle-to-direct conversion, 3-month retention by acquisition channel, and content viewing per rupee. Guardrails: premium tier churn, revenue per ad-free member, brand NPS among metro users, and ad load complaints.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: To close: 10x revenue in three years isn't credible in an Rs 38,000 crore market, but 10x reach is. Keep the premium top intact, open an ad-supported mass tier, borrow distribution from telcos, Flipkart and OEMs, and make regional India the core of the content slate. That turns Netflix from a metro luxury into India's second screen, with revenue growing about 3-4x and a path to profit by Year 3.

answer_and_recommendation: Reframe: 10x revenue (about Rs 40,000 cr) would exceed India's whole digital video market, so commit to 10x reach (about 20 mn to about 200 mn monthly active members) and about 3-4x revenue (about Rs 12,000-15,000 cr) by Year 3. Ranked levers: (1) Ad-supported price ladder - Rs 79-99 mobile-with-ads and Rs 149-199 TV-with-ads, keep ad-free plans and prices, annual UPI Autopay plans; the biggest unlock because price is the top funnel leak. (2) Distribution bundles - mass telco prepaid bundles on the ad tier, scale the Flipkart loyalty bundle (which helped drive record Q3 2026 India net adds), add smart-TV OEM, fibre and DTH partners. (3) Regional-first content - move South and other Indian languages to about 35-40% of hours via post-theatrical South films, dubbing in 8+ languages, and family-safe series for TV households; plus a vertical discovery feed and cricket-free live events. Phasing: Year 1 about 45-50 mn (ad tier, payments fixes, telco deal), Year 2 about 100-120 mn (OEM/fibre, regional originals, live events), Year 3 about 200 mn (India ad products, premium price rises). Risks and mitigation: brand dilution (low ad load, ad-free premium kept), inactive bundle members (activation-linked wholesale pricing, active-member North Star), content cost inflation (multi-year regional output deals), regulatory content risk (strong standards and practices under IT Rules 2021). Closing line: 'Netflix doesn't need to beat JioHotstar at cricket. It needs to be the second screen in every Indian home: premium at the top, ad-supported and bundled for Bharat, and that is how 20 million becomes 200 million.'
counter_metrics_guardrails: Guardrails: (1) ad-free member churn and revenue per ad-free member (cannibalisation check: downgrade rate to the ad tier under about 5%); (2) monthly active member share of total accounts, so bundled 'ghost' seats don't inflate the 10x (target above 70% active); (3) 3-month retention by acquisition channel (bundle vs direct vs ad tier); (4) ad load and ad complaint rate, ad tier NPS; (5) content cost per viewing hour, so regional spend doesn't outrun viewing; (6) payment failure and involuntary churn on UPI Autopay; (7) brand perception among metro premium users (brand tracker); (8) India contribution margin trajectory to break even by Year 3; (9) regulatory complaints and grievance-redressal SLA under IT Rules 2021.
follow_up_twists: Twist: 'Leadership insists on 10x revenue, not members.' Response: Show the TAM math (India video market is about Rs 38,000 cr), offer the closest credible path (3-4x India revenue plus India-made content exported globally, counting global viewing revenue attributed to Indian originals), and ask whether the goal is really India's strategic share.

Twist: 'IPL digital rights come up after 2027 - should Netflix bid?' Response: Only for a non-exclusive or global-rights slice at a disciplined price; a full IPL package (about Rs 23,000-24,000 cr for 2023-27 digital rights, paid by Viacom18) would consume years of India profit; better to buy cricket-adjacent events and documentaries.

Twist: 'Ads are delayed globally (ad revenue forecast cut to $2.7 bn) - what if you can't launch an India ad tier in Year 1?' Response: Lead with bundles and a Rs 99 mobile plan with lower resolution and a fixed one-device limit, then layer ads in Year 2; reach can still grow, but ARPU will be lower.
common_pitfalls: Accepting '10x revenue' at face value and building a feature list without a TAM sanity check; strong candidates show it exceeds the whole market and reframe.
Proposing to 'just cut prices' across all plans, which reprices the existing 20 mn base and destroys revenue; the answer is price discrimination via an ad tier and bundles.
Saying 'buy IPL/cricket rights' - they are locked with JioStar until 2027, cost far more than Netflix India's revenue, and are shared with Prasar Bharati for national-interest events.
Counting bundled accounts as success without an activity guardrail, and forgetting that Netflix no longer reports subscriber counts, so the North Star should be active members and engagement.
skills_tested: structuring, quant, business sense, prioritisation, empathy, communication
linked_teardown: None (closest relevant local research is meesho_product_teardown for Tier 2/3, mobile-first Bharat user behaviour; no Netflix-specific teardown folder exists)
